children.value: times. A model with too little capacity cannot capture the pattern in the data, and one with too much capacity also captures the noise. Two rules that predict whether it is warm show the extremes. A model that is too simple says: “if the sun is out, it is warm”. A model that is too complex says: “if the sun is out, and it is a summer month and we are in the northern hemisphere or a winter month and we are in the southern hemisphere, or we are near the equator, or in a desert that is not an ice desert, and it is not cloudy, raining, or snowing, and there is no strong wind, no solar eclipse, and no volcanic eruption, and we are not in the water, in a cave, in the shade, in an air-conditioned house or car, or in a freezer, then it is warm”.

Humans are good at finding the right level of abstraction. “Birds can fly” is a simple model, and we learn the exceptions, such as penguins, separately. The question of what makes a chair a chair has no simple answer in terms of shape, so we use an abstract concept: we can sit on it. Horses come in a narrow variety of forms, and we draw clear limits on what counts as a horse; donkeys, zebras, and giraffes do not. Dogs come in a wide variety of forms, yet we recognize them immediately.
shows the two failures for classification and regression.

occurs when the model is too simple for the pattern in the data, for example a straight line for a curved relationship. Its error is large already on the training data, and it predicts new data poorly.

occurs when the model follows the training data too closely, typically because it has too many parameters relative to the number of training examples. Its training error is small, but it fails on new data, because it has learned the noise of the particular sample. The optimal model has small errors on both the training data and new data.

The third is the noise in the data, which no model can remove. Reducing the bias by adding capacity usually increases the variance, and the reverse. The goal is therefore the model with the smallest sum of squared bias and variance.

An old heuristic for finding the right capacity is
Numquam ponenda est pluralitas sine necessitate

, “plurality must never be posited without necessity”. In its modern reading, it says that when several hypotheses explain the observations equally well, we should prefer the simplest one. Statistical learning refined the idea in the 20th century. For building models, it means starting with low capacity and adding capacity only as far as the task requires. Physics offers an example: Newton’s laws simplify the real world, yet they are accurate enough in many situations.

Simpler models generalize better, but a model must not be so simple that its training loss stays high. Modern language models have billions of parameters, enough to memorize large parts of their training data.
keeps them from doing so by penalizing complex models;

describes the methods. L2 regularization, for example, adds a penalty for large weights to the loss, so the network prefers many small weights over a few large ones, and L1 regularization drives many weights to exactly zero.
